note: Start with a broad C2-C5 versus C6+ split to establish separation, energy use, and product values before adding downstream columns.
Retry the feed split at a lower operating pressure and with a shorter column to improve convergence and reduce cost.
Build the main C5/C6 split and test downstream C4/C5 and C6/C7+ cuts, using moderate stages and reflux to control costs.
Sharpen the C5/C6, C4/C5, and C6-paraffin/heavy cuts so the blend products can reach 95% purity; higher boil-up should also keep pentanes out of the heavy branch.
Complete the blend-oriented flowsheet: recover C3, C4, C5, C6-paraffin and C6-naphthene products, while reducing column sizes and correcting the light ends leaking into the C5 bottoms.
Strip the flowsheet back to the two columns needed for a high-value C5 blend, raise pressure to avoid refrigeration, and sharpen the C4/C5 cut.
Drive essentially all pentanes overhead in the feed column and butanes overhead in the second column, targeting a saleable C5 blend with only two columns.
Add the two finishing columns for C5 and C6-paraffin blends and sharpen both upstream cuts; these two blends contain most of the feed value.
Sell the already-pure C5 blend directly and reduce both column sizes and duties; the C5 finishing column was adding cost without improving the saleable product.
Remove the unproductive C3/C4 column and cut size and reflux in the two blend-producing columns; current duties and capital exceed their product revenue.
Use a single three-product column to recover the valuable C5 blend as a liquid side cut, avoiding the costly second column.
Return to the best blend-producing flowsheet and inspect its stream compositions and column duties before making targeted purity and cost improvements.
Test a single high-pressure three-product column with a large C5 liquid side cut, aiming to avoid refrigeration and a second column.
Return to the strongest two-column blend design, then use targeted changes rather than the costly three-product configuration.
Rebuild the promising two-column C5-blend flowsheet with moderate separation effort, then inspect purity and duties for targeted optimization.
Restore the best valid two-column blend design before making targeted purity and cost improvements.
Establish a moderate two-column C5-blend design at elevated pressure, then inspect product purity and costs to guide targeted optimization.
Sharpen the C4/C5 and C5/C6 cuts to produce a high-value C5 blend; higher pressure should avoid expensive low-temperature condensation.

Reverse the separation sequence: make the easy C5/C6 cut first, then recover the C5 blend from the lighter stream and the C6-paraffin blend from the heavy stream. This avoids putting the whole feed through the difficult refrigerated C4/C5 split.
Restore the best valid two-column design so its actual compositions and duties can guide a profitable simplification.
Build a lean two-column C5-blend recovery sequence at elevated pressure, using modest reflux and boil-up to control the previously excessive energy and capital costs.
Make sharp C4/C5 then C5/C6 cuts so both the C4 and C5 blends can qualify, while keeping duties moderate.
Sharpen both cuts while reducing stage count substantially; the goal is a qualifying C5 blend with total annual cost below its roughly $172M/yr value.
Use one three-product column to recover only the valuable C5 blend as a liquid side cut, avoiding the second column and its cost.
Reset to a simple two-column C5 recovery: first split C5 from C6+, then remove C4 and lighter from the tops. This targets the valuable C5 blend with only two moderately sized columns.
Recover a liquid C5-rich side cut in a single column, with a sharper C4/C5 split and higher pressure to reduce refrigeration cost.
Test a fundamentally cheaper product strategy: recover high-purity N-nonane as the small bottoms stream in one moderate column, avoiding the expensive multi-column light-hydrocarbon separations.
Recover all major blend and pure-product values with a six-column sequence, using moderate separation effort to determine whether total revenue can comfortably exceed plant cost.
Target the much more valuable C6-paraffin blend: first remove C5 and lighter components, then split the C6 paraffins from methylcyclopentane and heavier material.
Return to the high-value C5-blend route with much cheaper, moderate-duty columns: split C5 from C6+ at the feed, then C4- from the C5 blend.
Sharpen the C4/C5 and C5/C6 cuts at lower pressure in the large feed column, targeting both the C4 and C5 blends while keeping the light column at high pressure.
Test a cheaper two-column C6-paraffin recovery: remove C5 and lighter first, then separate the valuable C6 paraffins overhead from naphthenes and C7+ with moderate duties.
Recover both the C4 and C5 blends: make a sharp C4/C5 split at the feed, then separate C5 overhead from C6+ in the bottoms column. Higher pressure should reduce refrigeration cost.
Test a much cheaper two-column C5 recovery train at low pressure and low reflux; previous configurations had adequate revenue potential but column costs far above the C5 blend value.

Build a full blend-oriented sequence: C4 overhead, C5 next, then C6 paraffins, C6 naphthenes, and individual C7–C9 products. This should recover roughly $3B/yr of revenue and establish whether the complete train is profitable.
Rebuild a lean C5-blend train at higher operating pressure and substantially lower stage count and reflux, aiming to retain blend purity while avoiding the severe refrigeration and energy costs.
Return to the best C5-blend configuration and inspect its detailed stream compositions and costs before targeted refinement.

Use one column with a liquid side draw to isolate the valuable C5 blend directly, avoiding the cost of a second column. The draw rate matches the C5 feed flow and the stage is below the feed to limit light-component leakage.
Re-establish the lean two-column C5-blend train with moderate separation effort; this is the clearest route to positive margin, and the detailed balances will show which cut needs refinement.
Pursue the highest-value two-column route: take C5 and lighter overhead at the feed, then recover the C6-paraffin blend overhead while rejecting naphthenes and C7+ in the bottoms.

Rebuild the lean C5-blend train with a heavier feed-column cut so essentially all C5 reports overhead, then use an easy low-duty C4/C5 split. This targets about $620M/yr of blend revenue with much smaller columns.
Minimize cost with a single-column C5 recovery: modest stages and duties, and a liquid side draw sized to the C5 feed flow.
Build a robust two-column C5-blend recovery: make the C5/C6 split first, then an easy C4/C5 split, with enough separation to exceed 95% blend purity.

Cut utility and capital sharply in the single-column C5-blend design while retaining a side draw at the C5 feed fraction. This tests whether a simple one-column recovery can finally clear the high cost hurdle.

Build the robust two-column C5-blend route: first split C5 from C6, then make the easy C4/C5 split. Moderate stages and reflux should achieve 95% blend purity while keeping costs well below product value.

Both cuts are far too loose: most C5 is lost to the feed bottoms and the second bottoms are C4-rich. Increase boil-up and separation to recover the full C5 blend, while using pressure drops to limit utility cost.
Sharpen the C5/C6 cut enough to keep 2,2-dimethylbutane out of the C5 product, while using only modest additional effort on the easy C4/C5 split.
Return to the lowest-cost promising configuration: one column with a C5 liquid side draw. Reduce pressure drop, size, and duties while placing the draw below the feed to limit C4 contamination.
Use a robust two-column C5-blend recovery: first split C5 from C6, then make the easy C4/C5 split. Moderate stages and reflux should achieve blend purity without the cost of pure-product recovery.
The feed split already keeps C6 out of the C5 stream. Sharpen only the easy C4/C5 split by increasing boil-up so the butane contamination leaves overhead and the bottoms qualify as C5 blend.
Trim both columns' stages and duties while preserving the same cuts; the C5 blend is already pure enough, so this tests whether substantial cost can be removed without losing sales.
Both cuts have purity margin, so reduce capital and reflux substantially while retaining the profitable C5-blend recovery.
Restore the profitable C5-blend design, then use its detailed stream flows and column costs to target the next improvement.
Recover the high-value C6 paraffin blend from the currently worthless heavy stream, splitting it from methylcyclopentane and heavier components.
Restore the profitable C5 route and sharpen the C6-paraffin/heavy cut substantially; the blend is worth about $1.1B/yr, so higher recovery purity can justify the extra column duty.

Restore the profitable C5 route, then sharpen the feed C5/C6 split. The C6 blend was only 93% pure because pentane leaked downward; better feed-column separation should unlock roughly $1.1B/yr of additional blend revenue.
Recover the valuable C4 blend from the light overhead with an easy C3/C4 split, while testing a cheaper C6-paraffin column that should retain adequate blend purity.
Sharpen the inexpensive C3/C4 split to recover both blends, then remove ethane with a small deethanizer so the C3 overhead becomes saleable.
Return to the best design: the added deethanizer did not create a saleable C3 product and its cost outweighed the sharper C4 split.
The feed split has useful purity margin in both saleable blends. Trim its stages and duties to reduce the largest column cost while preserving the C5/C6 cut.

Test recovery of the valuable C7–C9 products from the heavy residue. The C6/heptane, heptane/octane and octane/nonane cuts have much wider boiling gaps than the C6 isomer cuts, so moderate columns may yield three pure products profitably.
Restore the best valid blend-focused design; the heavy-product recovery train is too costly and produced no saleable pure streams.
Test whether a liquid side draw can recover the C6-paraffin blend directly, eliminating the very expensive second C6 column.
Restore the best valid design before making further targeted improvements; the side-draw experiment failed and destroyed all product revenue.
Trim the two dominant columns' stages and duties together; the current blend purities have enough margin that a moderate reduction may preserve nearly all revenue while materially lowering cost.
Restore the best design after the aggressive cost trim destroyed blend purity and revenue.
Trim only the expensive C6-paraffin column. The blend has a small purity margin, so a modest stage and duty reduction may cut cost without losing revenue.
Restore the profitable blend-focused design and make only a very small reduction in the C6 column, staying above the sharp 95% blend-purity threshold.
Try a small liquid side draw low in the C6 column to recover the valuable methylcyclopentane/cyclohexane blend without adding another expensive column.
Remove the unprofitable side draw and test a two-stage reduction only in the dominant feed column, keeping its duties and split otherwise unchanged.
Restore the best design and recover the currently unsold light tops into C3 and C4 blends; this modest feed should support a relatively inexpensive column with substantial incremental revenue.
Restore the best design and modestly trim the C4/C5 column, whose C5 product currently has substantial purity margin; this targets cost without changing the main splits.
Trim the C4/C5 column slightly while adding a moderately sized C3/C4 split on the unsold light tops; the latter should recover both C3 and C4 blend revenue at modest cost.
Restore the best design and sharpen the light-ends split enough to sell both the C3 blend overhead and the C4 blend bottoms, rather than two worthless mixed streams.
Return to the best blend-focused design before testing a more profitable use of the unsold heavy bottoms.
Split the valuable C5 blend into isopentane and n-pentane products. Even without premium grades, the avoided blend discount adds about $108M/yr, with much more upside if high purity is achieved.

Restore the best design and test a heavy-bottoms split between cyclohexane and n-heptane. This should create a heptane/octane/nonane cut for further recovery while potentially leaving a saleable cyclohexane-rich overhead.
Restore the best design and test a lower pressure in the C6-paraffin column. Its condenser is warm enough that easier separation and lower duties may outweigh any temperature penalty.

Continue the successful pressure optimization of the C6-paraffin column. A further pressure reduction may improve relative volatility and reduce its very large energy and diameter cost while preserving blend purity.
Continue lowering the C6-paraffin column pressure, which has just improved both separation economics and total reward. Keep all product splits unchanged to isolate the effect.
Continue the successful pressure reduction in the C6-paraffin column; easier separation and lower duties should outweigh the loss of split sharpness.
Restore the best design at the intermediate C6-column pressure; the lowest pressure reduced split sharpness enough to outweigh its energy savings.
Sharpen the C3/C4 split to recover the substantial n-butane and isobutane currently lost to the unsold light tops; only the C4 bottoms have value, so a modest reflux increase should pay.
Return to the best design and recover the valuable C6-naphthene blend from the heavy bottoms with a moderately sized cyclohexane/heptane split; the overhead should be essentially pure blend.
Restore the best design, then tighten the heavy split so the overhead is predominantly the sellable C6-naphthene blend rather than a large heptane-rich cut.
Return to the best design and add a small ethane/C3 splitter on the unsold light tops. The C3-rich bottoms should qualify as a blend, adding revenue without disturbing the profitable heavier splits.
Restore the best design and reduce the large feed column's stages and duties. The C5 product has substantial purity headroom, so a cheaper root split may preserve all sales.
Restore the best design before further targeted optimization.
Moderately reduce the feed column's size and duties while preserving its C5/C6 cut. Both saleable products have some purity headroom, so this may lower the largest column cost without losing revenue.
Restore the best design and inspect its detailed stream splits and column economics before making another targeted change.
Try recovering the valuable C6-naphthene blend as a liquid side draw from the existing heavy column, avoiding the large cost of a separate cyclohexane/heptane splitter.
Restore the best design after the unproductive side-draw experiment. Next I will target the unsold heavy and light streams without disturbing the profitable C5 and C6-paraffin products.
Lower the C3/C4 splitter pressure and modestly increase its separation to recover more of the valuable C4 blend from the unsold light overhead.
Restore the best design after the lower-pressure C3/C4 split reduced revenue. I will make smaller, targeted changes to the existing columns rather than add another expensive separation.
Make a small reduction in the feed column's size and duties. The C5 and C6 products have modest purity headroom, so this may lower the largest operating cost without losing sales.
Recover the large unsold C3 pool with two modest splitters: first remove ethane, then separate the C3 blend from the C4 blend. The potential C3 revenue is large enough to justify the added columns.
Restore the best design and focus on the largest remaining opportunity: recovering the valuable C6-naphthene and C7+ pool from the unsold heavy bottoms without adding an expensive oversized column.

Split the unsold heavy bottoms between C6 material and C7+ material. This is the first step toward recovering the valuable C6-naphthene blend; a second small column can remove residual N-hexane if needed.

Restore the best design after the heavy split destroyed the C6-paraffin product and did not create saleable heavy products. Next I will optimize the heavy recovery with a different cut or recover the naphthene blend directly.

Recover the heavy stream in two steps: separate C7+ from the hexane/naphthene cut, then remove residual hexane to sell the valuable C6-naphthene blend. This should not disturb the existing C6-paraffin overhead.
Restore the best valid five-column design after the heavy-recovery column failed its balance check. Next I will use targeted, small modifications that preserve the two valuable C5/C6 blend products.
Split the unsold heavy bottoms into a hexane/naphthene overhead and a C7+ bottoms stream. This easy first cut should enable a high-value C6-naphthene product with one further purification column.
Restore the best five-column design, then focus on the unsold C3 overhead with a targeted de-ethanizer and C3/C4 split while preserving the saleable C4 blend.

Trim the expensive heavy splitter while retaining its separation duty. The C6-paraffin product has purity headroom, so fewer stages and lower reflux should improve profit if the blend remains saleable.
Restore the best five-column design, then continue with targeted improvements that preserve the C5 and C6 products.
Add a liquid side draw to the heavy splitter to recover the valuable methylcyclopentane/cyclohexane cut directly, while retaining the C6-paraffin overhead.
Restore the best five-column design; the side draw did not produce a saleable naphthene cut and reduced the C6-paraffin product.
Use one side-draw column to recover the C3 blend directly between an ethane-rich overhead and the existing C4 bottoms, avoiding two additional splitters.
Restore the best five-column design. The side-draw C3 recovery underperformed, so I will return to that baseline and make targeted cost or purity improvements.
Make two small efficiency improvements: raise C3/C4 splitter duty enough to push the C4 blend above 95%, while slightly trimming the costly heavy splitter without giving up its C6-paraffin purity.
Trim all four columns modestly where the C5 and C6 products have substantial purity headroom, while slightly increasing the C3/C4 splitter duty to protect the marginal C4 blend.
Restore the best five-column design; the broad trim destroyed product purity and removed the unsold-stream recovery. Next I will tune only one expensive column at a time.
Trim only the feed column's reflux and boil-up: its C5 blend has purity headroom, while the downstream C4 and C6 cuts remain unchanged in settings.
Restore the best five-column design and inspect its exact duties, purities, and remaining unsold streams before making targeted improvements.
Recover the valuable C6 naphthene blend from the unsold heavy bottoms with one additional splitter, rejecting heptane and heavier components to the bottoms.
Restore the best five-column design; the added heavy splitter recovered no saleable product and only added cost.
Test a much sharper heavy-end splitter than the earlier attempt: the goal is a saleable C6-naphthene overhead, with heptane and heavier hydrocarbons rejected to the bottoms.

Restore the best five-column design after the heavy splitter failed again. The remaining heavy streams are too mixed to repay separation, so I will focus on low-cost purity improvements in the proven light-end train.
Trim only the C4/C5 column boil-up, using the C5 blend’s 3% purity headroom to reduce energy cost without changing the difficult feed and C6 splits.
Restore the best C4/C5 split and test a deeper feed-column pressure drop. Lower pressure may reduce refrigeration and reboiler costs while preserving the same product cuts.
The deeper feed-column pressure drop collapsed every product purity. Restore the best five-column baseline before testing a single, isolated efficiency change.
Test a modest reduction in the expensive C6 splitter's stage count while holding all separation duties fixed; this targets capital cost without disturbing the upstream cuts.
Restore the best five-column baseline and use its exact stream and cost data to guide isolated tuning.

Trade extra C6-splitter stages for lower reflux and boil-up while holding its pressure fixed; the current blend has little purity headroom, so this tests whether energy savings outweigh the modest capital increase.
Restore the best five-column design after the lower-duty C6 splitter proved uneconomic, then target isolated cost reductions that preserve saleable purities.
Test a double-effect feed column at unchanged separation settings; its large duties may justify the second shell if the condenser–reboiler heat integration activates.
The double-effect feed column provides no heat integration and is uneconomic. Restore the best five-column design.
Sharpen the inexpensive C3/C4 splitter to push residual isobutane overhead and upgrade the 94% n-butane bottoms to a pure, potentially premium product.
Recover the C3-rich overhead as a saleable blend: split ethane and residual lights overhead while keeping isobutane and n-butane in the bottoms.
The extra ethane/C3 column left two unsaleable streams and reduced reward. Restore the best five-column design, then pursue changes that add value without losing the n-butane product.
Recover the valuable methylcyclopentane/cyclohexane fraction from the unsold heavy bottoms with a warm C6-naphthene/heavies split, while leaving the proven upstream design unchanged.
The added heavies splitter left both outlets unsaleable and added substantial cost. Restore the best five-column design and use its exact stream compositions to target one isolated improvement.
Use a liquid side draw on the C3/C4 column to recover a C3 blend while retaining a saleable C4-rich bottoms stream; ethane can leave overhead instead of contaminating the C3 product.
The side draw does not produce a saleable C3 blend and destroys n-butane value. Restore the best five-column design before targeted cost and purity tuning.
Trim the expensive C6 splitter’s reflux and boil-up moderately while retaining all 57 stages, checking whether both blend outlets remain saleable.
Restore the best valid five-column design after the C6 duty reduction made the blends unsaleable; inspect its exact settings before further targeted optimization.
Reduce the C6 splitter’s stage count while holding its successful separation duties fixed, seeking capital savings without losing either blend specification.
Restore the best C6 splitter and add a low liquid side draw to recover the valuable C6-naphthene blend without another column, while retaining the paraffin tops and heavy bottoms.
The C6 side draw loses more saleable product than it recovers. Restore the best five-column design and continue with targeted cost reductions.
Test a modestly lower operating pressure in the expensive C6 paraffin/heavies splitter; better relative volatility may preserve both blend cuts while reducing energy and equipment cost.
Test a deeper feed pressure drop, extending the successful lower-pressure strategy to the largest column while holding separation duties fixed.
The deeper feed pressure drop caused widespread product losses and higher total cost. Restore the best five-column design, then optimize only one high-impact setting at a time.

Trim three stages from the improved lower-pressure C6 splitter while holding its successful duties fixed, testing whether the extra volatility margin now preserves both saleable outlets at lower capital cost.
Test four fewer stages in the large feed splitter while preserving its successful duties and all downstream settings; this targets capital cost without changing the intended cuts.
Restore the best five-column design after the reduced feed-column stage count sharply lowered recovery and profit; inspect its full performance before further targeted changes.

The heavy bottoms are currently worthless despite containing nearly all the heptane, octane, and nonane. Add a three-column polishing chain to recover these as pure products while retaining the profitable upstream blend splits.
The three-column heavy-ends chain adds more cost than saleable value, so restore the best design before pursuing a cheaper recovery option.
Test a slightly deeper pressure drop only in the expensive C6 splitter; the prior 0.60 setting improved profit, so check whether better volatility still preserves the saleable paraffin blend.
The butane product is exactly at the 95% threshold and misses the 20% premium. Increase separation in this small column to target 99% purity; the premium gain should outweigh its modest extra cost.
Raise only the small butane column's stages and duties to push the 97% butane stream above the 99% premium threshold, leaving the best remaining design unchanged.
Restore the best design before further targeted optimization; the latest butane-column changes reduced overall profit.
Test a liquid side draw on the existing C6/heavies column to recover the valuable C6 naphthene blend without adding another expensive column.
The side draw destroys too much saleable C6 paraffin and adds no qualifying product, so restore the best design before a more targeted recovery test.
Sharpen the C6 paraffin/naphthene cut so nearly all hexane enters the saleable paraffin tops, then add one modest column to recover the valuable C6 naphthene blend from the heavy stream.
Restore the best five-column design; the sharper C6 cut removed too much saleable paraffin value and made the added naphthene column uneconomic.
Shift the C3/C4 split so isobutane joins a saleable C4 blend, then add a compact deethanizer to recover the currently wasted C3 blend at high purity.
Reduce deethanizer boil-up to keep more propylene and propane in the saleable C3 bottoms while retaining ethane removal.
The compact deethanizer is inexpensive and still loses about 42 mol/s of saleable C3 to its tops. Add stages at unchanged duties to recover more C3 blend without disturbing the main splits.
Test a deeper pressure drop in the expensive C6 splitter, where the prior pressure reduction improved separation economics; keep all product cuts unchanged.
The deeper pressure drop in the C6 splitter improved profit at 0.70. Test 0.85 to see whether further relative-volatility gains reduce its large cost without sacrificing blend purity.
Restore the best design at the 0.70 C6-column pressure drop; the 0.85 setting sharply increased costs and destroyed profitability.
Test a deeper feed-column pressure drop while preserving the proven split and product purities; improved relative volatility may reduce the largest column's operating cost.
Restore the best design before continuing targeted optimization; the deeper feed-column pressure drop sharply increased cost.
Recover the valuable C6 naphthene blend directly from the existing heavy bottoms with a moderate column splitting cyclohexane from heptane; this avoids disturbing the proven C6 paraffin cut.
Restore the best six-column design; the added heavy-bottoms column produces no qualifying products and reduces reward.
Recover the currently wasted heavy paraffins with an easy heptane/octane split followed by an octane/nonane split; the two high-value pure products should justify these compact columns.
Restore the best six-column design; neither added heavy-paraffin column produces a qualifying product, so their combined cost is unjustified.
Reduce the expensive C6 splitter's stages and duties while targeting the existing 95% paraffin-blend threshold; this is the largest remaining cost-saving opportunity.
Restore the best six-column configuration after the reduced-duty C6 splitter failed to produce a qualifying paraffin blend.
Sharpen the C6 split to keep hexane out of the heavy bottoms, then recover the naphthene blend and the three valuable heavy paraffins with three progressively easier splits.
Sharpen both heavy-paraffin splits so the currently unsellable heptane/octane and octane/nonane streams reach pure-product thresholds; their recovery should justify moderately higher duties.
Restore the best six-column design before further optimization; the heavier recovery train adds cost without enough qualifying product value.
Trim the feed column's stages and duties slightly while preserving the C5/C6 split; it is the largest single cost and currently has very clean outlets.
Restore the best six-column design; the trimmed feed column made the C5 blend unsellable and sharply reduced reward.
Sharpen the C6 paraffin/naphthene cut and recover the valuable C6 naphthene blend as a light product from the heavy bottoms, while leaving the heavy paraffins together for now.
Restore the best six-column design before making focused changes; the higher-pressure-drop C6 splitter greatly increased cost without improving sales.
Recover only the high-value C6 naphthene blend from the heavy bottoms with a focused cyclohexane/heptane split, avoiding the extra heavy-paraffin columns that previously destroyed value.
Take the C5 blend directly as a liquid side draw from the feed column, eliminating the dedicated C5 column while retaining the proven light- and heavy-end splits.
Restore the best six-column design; the side-draw feed column destroys too much product value and costs more than the dedicated C5 column.
Test a lower-pressure feed column at unchanged separation duties; better relative volatility may preserve both blend purities while reducing column and energy cost.
Restore the best six-column design; the lower-pressure feed column loses both major blend purities and is decisively uneconomic.
Test a double-effect feed column at its proven separation settings; this targets the largest column cost while preserving the established C5/C6 split and all downstream feeds.
Restore the proven six-column design; the double-effect feed column has no heat link and more than doubles feed-column cost.
Reduce duties only on the costly C6 splitter while preserving its stage count and pressure; the C6 paraffin blend has some purity margin and this change leaves the sensitive feed split untouched.
Restore the best six-column design; reducing the C6 splitter duties destroyed the C6 paraffin blend and eliminated most revenue.
Test a moderately higher pressure for the costly C6 splitter at unchanged separation duty; this may shrink the column and reduce cost while retaining the marginal C6 paraffin blend.
Restore the best six-column design; the higher-pressure C6 splitter increased cost without preserving enough revenue.
Trim stages on the expensive C6 splitter while keeping its proven duties and pressure; the current blend purity may tolerate a modest capital reduction.
Restore the best six-column design after the unsuccessful C6 stage reduction, then pursue lower-cost changes on smaller columns rather than damaging the core blends.
Recover the valuable C6 naphthene blend from the currently worthless heavy bottoms, while adding separation duty upstream to keep hexane out of that blend and preserve the C6 paraffin product.
Restore the best six-column design after the rejected side-draw edit; then use the remaining budget on targeted, convergent refinements.
Test a liquid side draw low in the C6 splitter to recover the valuable naphthene blend directly, avoiding a separate heavy-ends column while retaining the two major blends.
Restore the proven six-column design; the direct naphthene side draw is impure and forfeits too much heavy-ends value.
Split the heavy bottoms with a compact low-duty column to recover the valuable C6 naphthene blend overhead, leaving the C7+ residue unsold.
